# King's Quest V for the Atari ST

An unofficial reconstruction of the Atari ST version of *King's Quest V: Absence Makes the Heart
Go Yonder!* that Sierra announced and then cancelled in 1991.

![Title screen running on an emulated Atari STE](media/title.png)

**Want to play?** Download the zip from [Releases](https://github.com/jarnalyrkar/KQ5ST/releases).
It holds a ready game folder for an Atari STE/ST hard disk, Hatari or Steem SSE, with
instructions in `READ_ME.TXT`.

## Why this project exists

Sierra On-Line announced an Atari ST version of King's Quest V in *Sierra News Magazine* for a
spring 1991 release. Sierra's Srini Vasan and Sierra UK pushed for continued Atari ST
development, but Sierra dropped Atari ST support entirely shortly afterwards and the port was
cancelled ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Quest_V)). According to
[Atarimania](https://www.atarimania.com/), the port was probably close to finished: the manual
even has loading instructions for the Atari ST. It was never released.

This project tries to give the ST the version it should have had. Sierra built its ST games
with the same SCI interpreter as its Amiga games, and the two machines share the 68000 CPU, so
the port takes the shipped Amiga version and makes it run on TOS:

- The Amiga interpreter (`Prog`) is converted hunk by hunk into a TOS program, with a few byte
  patches.
- A small **shim** stands in for the parts of AmigaOS and the Amiga hardware that the
  interpreter uses (exec, dos, graphics, the blitter, input, timers) on top of GEMDOS, XBIOS and
  the ST hardware.
- The **art** comes from the PC EGA version (16 colours, which matches the ST's 16-colour low
  resolution), merged into the Amiga resources so the Amiga game scripts still work.
- **Sound** goes through a new YM2149 driver that plays the music data the Amiga version
  shipped for 3-voice hardware.
- Small **script patches** fix speed, add mouse-only title skips, map the keypad as in the PC manual, and remove the copy protection (as in the later CD
  release).

It runs in Hatari (STE, TOS 1.62, 4 MB) and has been play-tested from the opening through the town,
the forest and the desert (oasis, temple, bandits' tent). See [`port/docs/HANDOFF.md`](port/docs/HANDOFF.md) for the current state and known gaps.

## What is in this repository

The repository holds **only the project's own work**: the shim, the patches, the tools and the
documentation. The original games, the generated game folder and other projects' code are not
included (see `.gitignore`).

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [`port/docs/`](port/docs/README.md) | Development notes, split by area. **Start with [`port/docs/README.md`](port/docs/README.md).** They cover how the interpreter is mapped onto TOS (`ARCHITECTURE.md`), art and screen (`GRAPHICS.md`), input (`INPUT.md`), game-script patches (`SCRIPTS.md`), the YM2149 sound driver (`SOUND.md`), a map of the Amiga interpreter (`AMIGA_PROG.md`) and how to build, test and debug (`WORKFLOW.md`). |
| [`port/st/src/`](port/st/src) | The TOS shim in C and 68000 assembly: AmigaOS libraries (`exec.c`, `dos.c`, `memory.c`), display and blitter (`display.c`, `blit.c`, `blitter.c`), IKBD input (`input.c`), YM2149 sound (`ym.c`), Roland MT-32 over MIDI (`mt32.c`), startup and trap glue (`glue.S`). |
| [`port/st/patches/prog.patch`](port/st/patches/prog.patch) | Byte patches applied to the Amiga interpreter during the build, with comments. |
| `port/st/build.sh`, `play.sh`, `run.sh` | Build `KQ5ST.PRG`; play in Hatari; headless test runs. |
| [`port/st/tests/`](port/st/tests) | Autoplay scripts for headless Hatari runs. |
| [`port/tools/`](port/tools) | Python tools: Amiga disk and hunk-file readers, a relocation-aware 68000 disassembler, an SCI resource extractor and script disassembler, picture/view converters, the art, script and sound patch builders, and the release packer. See [`port/README.md`](port/README.md). |

## Building from your own copy

You need the Amiga release of King's Quest V (version 1.000.000, eight ADF disk images) and the
PC EGA floppy release (version 0.000.055, disk images 1–9; the tenth image in some sets carries
a different `RESOURCE.MAP` and must be left out). Tools needed: Python 3 with
`Pillow` and `capstone`, `7z`, an m68k cross toolchain (`m68k-linux-gnu-gcc` and binutils;
`build.sh` sources `~/.local/opt/m68k-gcc/env.sh`, so edit that line for your setup) and
[Hatari](https://www.hatari-emu.org/) to run it. From `port/`:

```sh
# 1. Unpack the originals
for i in 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7; do python3 -I tools/adf.py ".../KQ5_Disk$i.adf" extracted/amiga_files/d$i; done
for f in .../dos/disk0[1-9].img; do 7z x -y -oextracted/dos_files "$f"; done   # not disk 10
python3 -I tools/sciextract.py extracted/amiga_files extracted/res_amiga
python3 -I tools/sciextract.py extracted/dos_files  extracted/res_dos
python3 -I tools/colourmap.py extracted/res_dos extracted/res_amiga extracted/amiga_files/d0/spal

# 2. Split and disassemble the Amiga interpreter (the docs refer to work/prog/disasm/hunkNN.s)
python3 -I tools/hunks.py extracted/amiga_files/d0/Prog work/prog
python3 -I tools/disasm.py work/prog work/prog/disasm

# 3. Game folder: the Amiga files, then the ST art, script and sound patch files
mkdir -p st/hd
cp extracted/amiga_files/d0/{RESOURCE.MAP,RESOURCE.000,resource.cfg,amiga3v.drv,amigasnd.drv,spal,version,756.SCR,756.TEX,9.pat} st/hd/
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7; do cp extracted/amiga_files/d$i/RESOURCE.00$i st/hd/; done
python3 -I tools/makest.py st/hd
python3 -I tools/makescr.py st/hd
python3 -I tools/makesnd.py st/hd

# 4. Build KQ5ST.PRG and play
st/build.sh
st/play.sh
```

`tools/mkrelease.sh VERSION` packs `st/hd` into `dist/KQ5ST-VERSION.zip` for a release.

The decompiled Amiga game scripts that the docs refer to (`amiga-decompiled/`, next to `port/`)
are sluicebox's [`sci-scripts`](https://github.com/sluicebox/sci-scripts) folder
`kq5-amiga-1.000.000`.

## Copyright and licences

**King's Quest V is © 1990 Sierra On-Line, Inc.** The rights now belong to Activision
(Microsoft). This is a non-commercial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Sierra,
Activision or Microsoft. If you enjoy the game, buy it (it is sold on GOG and Steam).

Copyrighted by Sierra and **not** covered by this project's licence:

- **The game data**: the `RESOURCE.*` files, `amiga3v.drv`, `amigasnd.drv`, `756.SCR`,
  `756.TEX`, `9.pat`, `spal`, `version` and `resource.cfg` in the release zip are copied
  unchanged from the Amiga release.
- **The interpreter**: `KQ5ST.PRG` in the release zip contains Sierra's Amiga interpreter `Prog`,
  converted and patched, linked with the project's shim.
- **The ST art, scripts and sounds**: the `N.p32`, `N.v32`, `N.SCR` and `N.snd` files in the
  release zip are Sierra's artwork, game scripts and music, converted or patched by the tools.
- **Excerpts in this repository**: `port/st/patches/prog.patch` quotes a few original bytes of
  `Prog` (to check that each patch hits the right place); `port/tools/makescr.py` and
  `port/tools/makesnd.py` quote short bytecode and sound-data sequences; the docs cite addresses,
  names and behaviour of the original program.

The project's own code (everything in this repository: shim, patches, tools, scripts and docs) is
licensed under the **GNU General Public License v3.0 or later** ([`LICENSE`](LICENSE)). Some
tools port logic from ScummVM's SCI engine (below), which is GPLv3+ as well.

## Built with

The project could not have been done without these:

- **[ScummVM](https://www.scummvm.org/)** (GPLv3+): its SCI engine was the reference for the
  resource formats, picture and view decoding and the interpreter's behaviour.
  `tools/sciextract.py`, `tools/scipic.py` and parts of `tools/sciview.py` port its logic.
- **[sluicebox/sci-scripts](https://github.com/sluicebox/sci-scripts)**: decompiled SCI source
  of the Sierra games, used to understand what each room and object does before patching it.
- **[Hatari](https://www.hatari-emu.org/)** (GPLv2+): the Atari ST/STE emulator used for all
  testing, including its debugger, profiler, NatFeats debug output and GEMDOS hard-disk
  emulation.
- **[Steem SSE](https://sourceforge.net/projects/steemsse/)**: Atari ST emulator.
- **[Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/)** (BSD): the 68000 disassembly in
  `tools/disasm.py`.
- **[GCC and GNU Binutils](https://www.gnu.org/)** (GPL): the m68k cross compiler, assembler and
  linker that build `KQ5ST.PRG`.
- **[Python](https://www.python.org/)** and **[Pillow](https://python-pillow.org/)**: all tools
  and image work.
- **[SoX](https://sourceforge.net/projects/sox/)** and **[FFmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/)**:
  recording and listening to sound output.

The development was done together with Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant.

# Dogs of War – Windows/Linux port at 60 fps


Gameplay video / Vídeo de gameplay

> **Repository layout** — `source/`: the complete C source (the game translated to C in `source/generated/`, the machine in `source/runtime/`, and the platform backends in `source/host/` and `source/port/`; see `source/README.md` for Windows and Linux builds). > `build/`: the ready-to-run files: `dowport.exe` (Windows) or `dowport` (Linux), `original/` (empty: you put your own game files there), `data/` (languages and support files), `shaders/`, `music/` and `default.json`. *Versión en español a continuación / Spanish version below: [Dogs of War – Port para Windows/Linux a 60 fps](#dogs-of-war--port-para-windowslinux-a-60-fps).* A native Windows and Linux port of **Dogs of War** (Atari ST, Elite 1989, Pera Putnik's HAGA version). The game's own 68000 program, translated to C, runs inside a small Atari STE machine and is drawn at your monitor's refresh rate: the game logic runs at 25 Hz and the port **interpolates between its frames**, so movement is smooth at 60 Hz (or 144 Hz…) with very low input latency. It is a single self-contained C program. **What it is.** The game's own 68000 program has been **translated entirely to C**, and it is compiled with a small Atari STE machine (mini-TOS, timers, keyboard and joystick, video, YM2149 sound chip) and a native Windows or Linux host into one executable. The original game logic runs unchanged at its own 25 Hz; the port draws the images in between. **What it is not.** It is not an emulator of the Atari ST: no 68000 instruction is interpreted, and no Atari ROM or TOS is needed. **Downloads:** [Windows x64 ZIP](https://github.com/voodatari/Dogs-of-War-Atari-ST-Recomp/releases/download/v1.3.0/Dogs-of-War-Atari-ST-Recomp-for-Windows-x64.zip) · [Linux x64 AppImage](https://github.com/voodatari/Dogs-of-War-Atari-ST-Recomp/releases/download/v1.3.0/Dogs-of-War-Atari-ST-Recomp-for-Linux-x64.appimage). **What it adds to the original** - Frame interpolation to the refresh rate of your monitor, sub-pixel sprites, and low-latency input and audio. - Modern video: OpenGL, aspect modes, scaling filters, CRT effects and external shaders. - Sound: chip synthesis, a choice of music (the Atari ST's own, the Amiga's from your own Amiga disk, or MP3 music packs with loop points), multichannel effects with stereo panning and volumes per type. - Replaceable graphics (graphics packs), three save slots and a "back to the mission map" command, redefinable controls with gamepad support, and menus in English and Spanish. - Corrections of enemy micro-stutters and of explosion glitches that only appear at high frame rates (all can be switched off). **What stays the same.** The game itself: missions, enemies, weapons, scoring and the timing of the game logic are those of the original. ## Contents 1. [Features](#features) · 2. [Quick start](#quick-start) · 3. [Controls](#controls) · 4. [Options menu](#options-menu) · 5. [Video](#video) · 6. [Sound and music](#sound-and-music) 7. [Motion and latency](#motion-and-latency) · 8. [Graphics packs](#graphics-packs) · 9. [Game fixes](#game-fixes) · 10. [Saving](#saving) · 11. [Files and folders](#files-and-folders) 12. [Configuration reference](#configuration-reference) · 13. [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) · 14. [How it works](#how-it-works) · 15. [Building](#building-from-source) · 16. [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md) ## Features - **60 fps and beyond**: frame interpolation of the 25 Hz game, optional sub-pixel sprite smoothing, and an optional game-speed mode that matches the refresh rate exactly. - **Low latency**: fast input polling (1000 Hz), low-latency audio output, tunable emulation margin. - **Video**: OpenGL output with four aspect modes, three scaling filters, built-in CRT effects (scanlines, phosphor mask, curvature, vignette, glow) and external RetroArch `.glsl` shaders. - **Sound**: YM2149 chip synthesis, a multichannel mixer for the sampled effects, stereo panning of effects by on-screen position, per-type volumes, and a choice of music: the Atari ST's own, the Amiga version's (from your own disk) or replacement **MP3 music packs**. - **Graphics packs**: every sprite, tile and fixed screen of the game is dumped to editable PNG sheets; a pack of full-colour replacements is drawn instead, with the original animation and interpolation. - **Controls**: keyboard and XInput gamepads (two players), fully redefinable, plus pad shortcuts for rocket launcher, grenade and hold position, and an optional **twin-stick** mode (left stick moves, right stick aims and fires). - **Saving**: the original game has no saves; the port adds three slots and a "back to the mission map" command. - **Fixes** for stutters and glitches that appear only at high frame rates (all can be switched off). ## Quick start 1. For Windows and a standalone Linux build, put one of these data files directly in the existing `original\` / `original/` folder next to the executable. The Linux AppImage can read either `DOW` (Pera Putnik's HDD conversion, CRC32 `6703B50F`) or `Dogs of War (1989)(Elite)[cr Replicants][t].st` (CRC32 `F6E84D7A`) from `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dogs-of-war/original/`, normally `~/.local/share/dogs-of-war/original/`; set `DOW_ORIGINAL_DIR` to use another folder. - **Hard-disk data:** name it `DOW` (no extension); reference CRC32: `6703B50F`. The file is in the `FILES` folder of the Pera Putnik hard-disk version. - **Replicants disk image:** `Dogs of War (1989)(Elite)[cr Replicants][t].st`; CRC32: `F6E84D7A` (829,440 bytes). Put it in the `original` folder. The port detects the image by CRC32, so another `.st` filename with that same CRC also works. If both files are present, `original/DOW` takes priority. The Replicants image is read directly. 2. Run `dowport.exe` (Windows) or `./dowport` (Linux). While it loads, a **startup screen** lists the files that were found and are going to be used, with a progress bar; it goes on by itself two seconds after loading ends, or at once with a fire button (the **Startup screen** option of the System tab turns it off). On the first start it prepares, in a few seconds, `assets/original/` (the graphics dump, see [Graphics packs](#graphics-packs)); the bar follows that work. If the game data is missing, the game's own window says so and tells you which file goes in which folder; put it there and start the program again. 3. Press **Esc** (or the pad's **Start**) for the options menu. The Linux AppImages and `.tar.xz` packages include SDL2, so the system SDL2 package is not required at runtime. SDL selects the available audio backend automatically: desktop Linux normally uses its PulseAudio-compatible service (including PipeWire's compatibility layer), while systems without it can use another SDL backend such as ALSA. Set `SDL_AUDIODRIVER` only to override SDL's selection. ## Controls Every key and pad button can be redefined (see below); these are the defaults. | Action | Keyboard | Gamepad | |---|---|---| | Move | Cursor keys | Left stick or D-pad (fixed) | | Aim and shoot (twin-stick) | – | Right stick, 8 directions: the soldier faces and shoots that way whatever direction he is moving; it also holds fire while pushed (see below) | | Fire | Ctrl (left or right), Z | A, right trigger | | Next weapon | A | RB | | Previous weapon | – | LB (the game only cycles forward; the port jumps straight to the previous category) | | Quick rocket launcher | – | B: fires the first rocket launcher you bought that still has ammo (RPG-7, L.A.W., M.A.W.), then returns to the weapon you held | | Quick grenade | – | X: throws a hand grenade (if you bought any), then returns to the previous weapon | | Hold position | – | Left trigger: the soldier stands still while the stick still turns him, so you can shoot in any direction | | Menus / shop | 1, 2, Space, Enter… (passed to the game as Atari scancodes) | A also accepts in the shop; in "1 OR 2 PLAYER GAME?" it acts as key 1 (pad 1) or 2 (pad 2) | | Options menu | **Esc** (inside it, Page Up / Page Down or Tab change tab) | **Start** (B also closes it; L1 / R1 change tab) | | Leave the mission | – | Back (outside a mission it returns to the title screen) | | Fullscreen | F11 | – | | Emulation margin | Page Up / Page Down (`lat` in the window title) | – | | Reload graphics pack | F9 | – | | Quit | Alt+F4 | – | The first pad is player 1 (added to the keyboard) and the second pad is player 2; pads are detected when plugged in. **Twin-stick mode** (*Controls → Twin-stick: right stick aims*, on by default; off = the original single-stick control): the left stick moves the soldier and the right stick sets where he **faces and shoots**, in 8 directions (45° sectors, 40 % dead zone), whatever way the left stick is moving him: walk up while firing right, strafe while shooting diagonally… When the right stick is released he faces the way he walks again. While the right stick is pushed the original "fire without a direction = stand still" lock is released, so you can start moving without stopping the fire. *Right stick also fires* (on by default) holds the fire button for you while the right stick is pushed; turn it off to aim with the right stick and fire with the usual button. It only acts during a mission, and it uses pad 1 for player 1 and pad 2 for player 2. *Hold position* (left trigger) still works. **Redefining**: the *Controls* tab of the options menu shows a picture of the gamepad and the option *Redefine keys and gamepad buttons…*, which opens a window with every action. Select an action and press the new key or pad button: **Esc** cancels, **Delete** leaves it unassigned, and a key already used by another action is taken from it. *Restore default controls* resets everything. **Typing**: on the screens that ask for text (the name in the high-score table) every letter A–Z (including **Z**, which is also the second fire key, and **V**), the digits, Backspace, Delete and the usual punctuation keys are passed to the game. | Tab | Contents | |---|---| | **Game** | Back to the mission map · Save slot (1–3, with date) · Save game · Load game · Restart game (back to "1 OR 2 PLAYER GAME?", skipping the intro) · Invulnerability · Infinite money (both always off at start-up) | | **Sound** | Sound on/off · Volume · Music (Amiga / packs) · Music (YM2149F) · Sampled FX · FX (YM2149F) · Multichannel FX · FX stereo panning · Music | | **Video** | Fullscreen · Aspect ratio · Shader source · Scaling filter · Shader / CRT effect and its controls · Graphics pack | | **Motion** | Frame interpolation · Sub-pixel smoothing · Game speed · and, under *Latency*: Fast input polling · Low-latency audio · Audio sync trim | | **Controls** | Twin-stick: right stick aims · Right stick also fires · Redefine keys and gamepad buttons (opens a window, with *Restore default controls*) · picture of the gamepad (drawn by the program from the current controls) | | **System** | Language · Startup screen · Restore default options (reloads `default.json`) · Credits · Continue · Quit | ### Languages The texts of the menus (and the messages they show) are read from `data\languages\*.xml`; the program ships with **English** and **Spanish** and the language is chosen in **System → Language** (saved as `language`). To add a language copy `english.xml`, give the new file a different name, change `name` (what the menu shows) and `code` in its `` line and translate the text inside each `…`; never change an `id`, and keep codes such as `%d` or `%s` (the program fills them in). The new language appears in the menu at the next start. A string missing from a file is shown in English. ## Video - **Aspect ratio**: original 4:3, square pixels 16:10, stretch, or integer scale. - **Scaling filter**: sharp, smooth, or sharp bilinear. - **Shader / CRT effect**: none, scanlines, soft CRT, full CRT, or an external shader. Scanline, phosphor-mask, curvature, brightness, vignette and glow controls apply to the built-in ones (greyed out with an external shader). - **How it is drawn**: each frame is composed at integer scale (960×600) and one OpenGL pass scales it and applies the effect; if OpenGL is not available a software output is used. Shaders see a 320×200 screen (`InputSize` and, for external shaders, `TextureSize`), so scanlines match the game's lines, while the texture keeps more resolution for sub-pixel movement. - **Shader source**: what the shaders start from. *Scaled* is the behaviour above. *320x200 averaged* and *320x200 exact* always give the shaders the original 320×200 grid (averaged: each pixel is the mean of its block, so sub-pixel movement shows as blended colours; exact: one sample per block). Saved as `shader_source` (0, 1, 2). - **Fades**: the darkening that the game does at the end of a mission (it subtracts 1 from every component of its 512-colour palette) is drawn as a smooth, lighter dimming with the original colours at full 8-bit precision. - **External shaders**: copy **single-pass** `.glsl` files in RetroArch/libretro format (`#if defined(VERTEX) … #elif defined(FRAGMENT)`) into `shaders/`; they appear as "External: name". `MVPMatrix`, `Texture`, `InputSize` (320×200), `TextureSize`, `OutputSize`, `FrameCount` and the `#pragma parameter` values are provided. Multi-pass presets (`.glslp`, `.slangp`) are not supported. ### Shaders and licences **Resolution independence.** The phosphor mask of the built-in CRT effects and of every supplied shader is drawn at its original size (3 pixels per phosphor triad) at 1080 lines and grows in proportion to the picture height above that, so the phosphors look the same at 1080p, 1440p, 4K or any resolution in between (below 1080 lines it stays at 3 pixels). Each screen pixel averages the mask over its own area, so a non-integer scale produces no moire. This applies to `fakelottes`, `fakelottes-geom`, `crt-pi` and `fake-CRT-Geom` (the last one: its *Mask Size* parameter is multiplied by the same factor); `crt-nes-mini` has no mask and its scanlines come from the game's own lines, so it needed no change. The scanlines of all of them already follow the game's lines at any resolution. If you add shaders of your own whose mask is measured in screen pixels, scale it by `max(1.0, OutputSize.y / 1080.0)` the same way. The `.glsl` shaders supplied in `shaders\` were **not written for this program: they come from the RetroArch / libretro shader collection** ([glsl-shaders](https://github.com/libretro/glsl-shaders)), and each one keeps the authorship and licence of its author. Look at the top of every file: for example `crt-pi.glsl` (davej) is under the GNU GPL version 2 or later, and several files give only the author's name and no licence text, so check their upstream licence before redistributing them. The program only loads them at run time, as separate files, and nothing in it is derived from them; the built-in effects (Scanlines, Soft CRT, Full CRT) are this program's own code. If you redistribute the program with these shaders, keep their headers and licences with them. Their licences apply to those files only, not to the rest of the program. If you prefer not to ship them, delete the files: the program works without them and the built-in effects stay. ## Sound and music - **Chip sound**: the YM2149 (3 tones, noise, envelope) is synthesised from the game's register writes with their time stamp inside the frame, so it stays in sync with the picture. The music tempo is the one the game programs on MFP timer C (≈48.6 Hz), independent of the frame rate. - **Volumes**: overall *Volume* plus four sliders: *Music (Amiga / packs)* (the Amiga disk's music and the packs'), *Music (YM2149F)* (the Atari ST's original songs), *Sampled FX* and *FX (YM2149F)* (effects the chip itself makes). Each one is a gain applied while the sound is mixed, so they move smoothly. - **Multichannel FX** (off by default): the original plays effect samples on chip channels A and B (one voice each) and a new sample cuts the previous one. With this option the program mixes them: up to 8 voices at the original rate (4915.2 Hz) and 4-bit levels, read sample-and-hold like the chip. Different effects never cut each other; at most 2 instances of the *same* sample play at once (a third fades out the oldest in 10 ms), which stops gunfire and chained explosions from piling up. A soft limiter prevents clipping. - **FX stereo panning** (off by default): each effect is placed between the speakers by the horizontal position of the object that makes it (enemy, vehicle, explosion, your weapon…) when the sound starts: left edge of the play area 100 % left, centre both equally, right edge 100 % right (linear). Unknown origins are centred. Works with or without *Multichannel FX*. ### Music: Atari ST, Amiga and music packs The **Music** item of the Sound tab is a single list that goes through every music there is: - **Atari ST (original)**: the game's own chip music. It is always there and needs nothing. - **Amiga**: the music of the Amiga version, when its disk is in the `original/` folder (see below). - **The music packs** you put in `music/` (MP3; OGG and WAV also work): every **subfolder** with songs is a pack (e.g. `music/arrange/`); songs loose in `music/` form the pack "(music folder)". The list is rescanned each time the menu opens. When you rotate through it the new music **joins the song where the Atari ST's one is** (about; the original music keeps running silently underneath), instead of starting from the beginning. File names inside a pack: | File | Replaces the chip music of… | |---|---| | `mission.mp3` | song 0: intro, title screen and missions | | `map.mp3` | song 1: the mission map | | `endlevel.mp3` | song 6: end-of-level jingle (plays while the money is added up) | | `bonus.mp3` | song 3: the bonus screen that follows | | `fail.mp3` | song 7: game over | | `highscores.mp3` | song 5: the high-score table | | `song2.mp3`, `song4.mp3`, `song8.mp3`… | the remaining song numbers | - **Loop points**: a song can have a text file with the same name next to it (`mission.txt` for `mission.mp3`) that says where its loop goes: ``` Loop point start = "4345980863" Loop point back = "230030420" ``` The numbers are samples of the file **at its own sample rate** (44100 Hz, 48000 Hz…), counted from the start of the file. The song plays from the beginning; when the playback reaches `Loop point start` it jumps back to `Loop point back` and repeats that stretch for as long as the song is needed. An empty file, a missing number, or points outside the song leave it as it was (the whole file in a loop; the last case is noted in `error.log`). It only applies to the songs that loop (`mission`, `map`, `highscores`, `song1`…); the ones that play once ignore it. - The music keeps playing while the options menu is open: the Atari ST chip music (the game's own music routine goes on running while the rest of the game stands still), the Amiga music and the music packs. The *mission failed* screen waits until its song has ended or a button is pressed. - With a pack chosen, every song that has a file plays from it and the chip version is muted meanwhile; **songs without a file keep the chip music**, so a single MP3 is enough. With **Atari ST (original)** only the chip music plays. Sound effects always stay. - `endlevel`, `bonus`, `fail` (and `song2`, `song4`) end by themselves in the original: their file plays **once, in full**, and the game waits for it to finish; pressing fire or any key while one of them plays fades it out (about 0.7 s) and the game goes on. `mission`, `map` and `highscores` **loop without a gap** (digital silence is trimmed at both ends and the audio is read as a ring buffer). - Files are decoded in the background, in order of use, right after start-up and whenever the pack changes. If a song starts before its file is ready, the chip music stays silent instead of leaking for a moment. ### Music of your Amiga disk If you also own the **Amiga** version, put its disk in the same `original/` folder as the game data: either the disk image (`.adf`) or the WHDLoad package (`.lha`). Nothing of it is included in this program. The **Music** list then offers **Amiga** next to the Atari ST's and the packs' (it is the one chosen when there is no `arrange` pack). The program reads the sound driver of the Amiga game from your file (its songs and samples; the files are recognised by their content, not by their names) and plays the music in real time **with the game's own sound driver**, the way the Amiga did, instead of from MP3 files. The eight songs follow the same rules as the packs' (looping, ending by themselves, skipping with a button, volume while the options menu is open). It was checked against the Amiga disk image `Dogs of War (1989)(Elite)[cr].adf` and the WHDLoad package of DJ Mike (v2.1). The driver steps at the 50.4 Hz of the Amiga's CIA timer, so it is about 0.75 % faster than recordings made at exactly 50 Hz. ## Motion and latency **Frame interpolation** (on by default) shows the frames between the game's own 25 logic steps. **Sub-pixel smoothing** draws sprites at their exact in-between position instead of rounding to a whole pixel (it adds no frames). With interpolation **off**, every game frame is shown as it is and the delay is much smaller, at the price of judder (60 Hz is not a multiple of 25, so frames alternate between 2 and 3 refreshes). **Game speed** removes that judder: *Original* keeps 25 fps; *Match screen refresh* runs the game at the frame rate that divides the refresh rate (60 Hz: 1.2× speed, 30 logic frames per second, each exactly 2 refreshes; 144 Hz: 48 VBL/s; 100 Hz: 50, exactly original). Music and samples keep their normal speed. **Latency options** (Latency): - **Emulation margin** (`latency`, default 3.6 frames; Page Up/Down while playing): how far the emulation runs ahead of the screen. Below about 3.6 the picture has to be extrapolated and the scroll "bounces" when it stops. - **Fast input polling**: keyboard and pads are read about 1000 times per second on their own thread instead of once per screen frame (up to 16 ms late). - **Low-latency audio**: small device buffers (about 10 ms through the Windows mixer); the sound is kept in step with the image, its total delay following the emulation margin. **Audio sync trim** (−100…100 ms) shifts the sound later (positive) or earlier (negative) if it does not line up on your PC. If the new output cannot be opened the normal one stays. ## Graphics packs **The dump.** `assets/original/` is a complete dump of the game's graphics, taken straight from the data the game decompresses into RAM, as editable PNG sheets in canonical order, with an `index.json` (frame number, content hash, memory address and data format of every cell) and its own `README.txt`. The program makes it by itself the first time it starts (it plays the game with scripted input: intro, title, map, shop and the 12 missions; a few seconds). Delete the folder to make it again. | Folder | Contents | |---|---| | `sprites/` | `player`, `enemy_1`/`enemy_2`, `shots` + `shots_b`, `fx`, `boom`, `turrets`, `vehicle_a..d`, `bullets`. One cell per frame, each with a transparent 4 px margin for soft shadows and glows | | `tiles/` | `ground_N` (64×32 blocks, also the textures of horizontal-scroll sections) and `objects_N` (16×16 object tiles) for each of the 3 tile sets | | `screens/` | fixed pictures as layers: `intro_jungle`, `intro_soldier`, `title_logo`, `map`, `shop`, `hud_left`, `hud_right` (+ `.idx.png` index layers) | | `levels/`, `reference/` | every vertical level assembled, and the 8×8 font; reference only | **Making a pack.** Create a folder next to the dump (e.g. `assets/mod/`) and copy into it, with the same relative path and name, only the sheets you want to change. Edit them in any pixel-art editor in RGBA (any number of colours, soft alpha; keep the sheet size or an integer multiple of it). A pack folder in `assets/` is used automatically, or choose it with **Graphics pack**; **F9** reloads it while playing. Only cells that differ from the dump are used; everything else is drawn with the original graphics. **The example pack `mod`.** It is the pack that is used by default. It contains pictures of the game itself, so it is not handed out: the program carries only what the pack *changes* (the positions and the new values of the changed pixels), and the first time it starts, right after making the dump, it makes `assets/mod/` by copying the dump and applying those differences. If the dump is not the one the differences were taken from, nothing is written (the log says so). It is only made when the folder does not exist, so a pack of that name that you edit is never overwritten; delete it to get the example back. **How it works.** The game's graphics are 16-colour bitplanes, so a 256-colour picture cannot be written back into its memory. Instead the presenter recognises each graphic by its *content* (the same drawing of colour indices is the same graphic in any mission) and draws your PNG at the same place, with the same animation and the 60 fps interpolation. Screens are layers that replace only the pixels still equal to the original layer's, so text, cursors and scores keep being drawn by the game. Palette fades dim the replacements too. Not replaced: text and digits, the weapon icon / counters / lives of the side panels, and the rare sprites cut by the screen edge. ## Game fixes On by default; `enemy_script_fix: false` runs the game exactly as it was. No game file is modified. - **Enemy script** (`$B0B8`): when an enemy's counter reaches 0 the routine loads the next order and **returns without moving the enemy that frame**, so every order (fire, turn, change animation) loses a frame of movement. Unnoticeable at 25 fps on an Atari; at 60 fps it shows as micro-stutters (it happens in Hatari too). The patch turns the `RTS` at `$B13E` into a `BRA.B` to `$B0C6`. Order durations are unchanged; enemies travel ~1 px more per order. - **Sound driver**: while a sample effect plays, the driver stops writing the registers of music channels A and B and the noise register. Three conditional jumps (`$41EE2`, `$41EF8`, `$41F32`) are patched so the music keeps playing, and the effect's own register writes go to a separate synthesiser channel. - **Explosions in horizontal-scroll levels**: the horizontal scroll step (`$49A0`) forgets the explosion list (`$1472`), so explosions and the big fireball stayed fixed on screen while the scenery scrolled. A hook right before that routine's `RTS` adds the missing step. - `scroll_fix` stabilises the horizontal scroll presentation (see [Configuration reference](#configuration-reference)). ## Saving The original game has no save feature, so the port stores full snapshots of the machine in `saves/`. Use **Game → Save slot / Save game / Load game** (3 slots, with date) from the map, the shop or in the middle of a mission. What is always saved is the **map before the current mission** (with the money and missions completed at that moment) and loading returns to that map. **Back to the mission map** does the same without a slot. ## Files and folders ``` dowport.exe the program original\DOW hard-disk data file (reference CRC32 6703B50F) — or original\Dogs of War (1989)(Elite)[cr Replicants][t].st Replicants disk image (CRC32 F6E84D7A) data\languages\ the texts of the menus, one XML file per language (english.xml, spanish.xml) default.json factory options (read when options.json is missing or on "Restore default options") options.json your options (written when the menu closes) shaders\ external .glsl shaders (from the RetroArch collection, see Shaders and licences) music\ music packs (one subfolder each) assets\original\ graphics dump (made at the first start) assets\\ graphics packs (e.g. assets\mod) saves\ save slots (.dows) and crash reports error.log diagnostics: unusual events, audio gaps ``` The Linux AppImage reads game data from `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dogs-of-war/original/` (normally `~/.local/share/dogs-of-war/original/`); set `DOW_ORIGINAL_DIR` to use another folder. ## Configuration reference `options.json` is written by the menu. The Linux AppImage reads either file from `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dogs-of-war/original/` (normally `~/.local/share/dogs-of-war/original/`) or its bundled `original/DOW` by default. - **No sound on Linux**: leave `SDL_AUDIODRIVER` unset so SDL can select an available backend (normally the desktop's PulseAudio-compatible service, including PipeWire, or ALSA). `error.log` records the selected driver. - **Sound crackles or lags**: raise the emulation margin (Page Up) or turn off *Low-latency audio*; `error.log` lists audio gaps. - **Judder at 60 Hz**: leave *Frame interpolation* on, or use *Game speed → Match screen refresh* with interpolation off. - **A graphics pack does nothing**: it only replaces cells that differ from `assets/original/`; delete that folder to rebuild the dump and check the sheet names and sizes. - **If the game state gets corrupted** (it jumps to garbage code) the port returns automatically to a snapshot from a few seconds earlier and writes `saves/crashN_inicio.dows`, `crashN_entradas.txt` and `crashN_fin.dows` (the snapshot, your inputs since then and the corrupt state) plus a report in `error.log`. ## How it works - **The game**: its 68000 program is translated to C (`source/generated/`, one C function per routine, running as cooperative fibers). If the game ever jumps to an address that is not game code (a corrupted state) the port goes back to a snapshot from a few seconds earlier and logs it (see Troubleshooting). - **The machine** (`tos.c`, `runtime/machine.c`): an Atari STE with a mini-TOS (just enough GEMDOS/BIOS/XBIOS for the game), IKBD/ACIA keyboard and joystick, MFP timers and per-scanline palette zones. At every start `boot.c` builds the memory the original loader (`RUNME.TOS` and `HAGA`) leaves when it jumps into the game. All the 68000 code, the loader's included, is already C, so the original data source is used only for game data; the few variables of the loader that the code reads are in the program. - **Scene capture** (`scene.c`): for every logic frame it records the background (circular scroll buffer), the HUD and every drawn object (enemies, player, bullets, explosions, vehicles…) with its position, and keeps a **sprite atlas**. - **Presenter** (`render.c`, `present.c`): draws any instant between two logic frames, with scroll and sprites at intermediate positions, enemy-motion filters and scroll stabilisation. - **Output**: `video.c` (Win32 + OpenGL 3.3), `ym.c`, `mixer.c`, `mp3.c` (vendored minimp3 / stb_vorbis / WAV reader), `audioout.c` (waveOut / WASAPI), `menu.c` (portable `port/ui2d.c`), `input.c` (XInput), `cfg.c`, `gfxpack.c`, `dump.c`. - **Verification**: the translation was checked against an independent 68000 emulator, instruction by instruction and frame by frame, over the 12 missions (whole 4 MB of RAM, sound registers and palette). ## Building from source Everything is in `source/` (see `source/README.md`). On Windows, install Zig, MinGW-w64 or Clang and run `source\build.bat`; it writes `build\dowport.exe`. On Debian/Ubuntu Linux, install `build-essential pkg-config libsdl2-dev` and run `bash source/build-linux.sh`; it writes `build/dowport`. ## Status Working: boot from the original files, title, menus, mission map, shop and all 12 missions with 60 fps interpolation on Windows and Linux. Los controles de líneas de escaneo, máscara de fósforo, curvatura, brillo, viñeteado y resplandor se aplican a los incorporados (aparecen atenuados con un shader externo). - **Cómo se dibuja**: cada fotograma se compone a escala entera (960×600) y una pasada de OpenGL lo escala y aplica el efecto; si OpenGL no está disponible se usa una salida por software. Los shaders ven una pantalla de 320×200 (`InputSize` y, en los shaders externos, `TextureSize`), de modo que las líneas de escaneo coinciden con las líneas del juego, mientras que la textura conserva más resolución para el movimiento subpíxel. - **Origen del shader**: de qué parten los shaders. *Escalado* es el comportamiento descrito arriba. *320x200 promediado* y *320x200 exacto* dan siempre a los shaders la cuadrícula original de 320×200 (promediado: cada píxel es la media de su bloque, así que el movimiento subpíxel se ve como colores mezclados; exacto: una muestra por bloque). Se guarda como `shader_source` (0, 1, 2). - **Fundidos**: el oscurecimiento que hace el juego al terminar una misión (resta 1 a cada componente de su paleta de 512 colores) se dibuja como un oscurecimiento suave y más ligero, con los colores originales a 8 bits de precisión. - **Shaders externos**: copia en `shaders/` ficheros `.glsl` de **una sola pasada** en formato RetroArch/libretro (`#if defined(VERTEX) … #elif defined(FRAGMENT)`); aparecen como «Externo: nombre». Se proporcionan `MVPMatrix`, `Texture`, `InputSize` (320×200), `TextureSize`, `OutputSize`, `FrameCount` y los valores de `#pragma parameter`. Los presets de varias pasadas (`.glslp`, `.slangp`) no están soportados. ### Shaders y licencias **Independencia de la resolución.** La máscara de fósforo de los efectos CRT incorporados y de todos los shaders incluidos se dibuja a su tamaño original (3 píxeles por tríada de fósforo) con 1080 líneas y crece en proporción a la altura de la imagen por encima de eso, de modo que los fósforos se ven igual a 1080p, 1440p, 4K o cualquier resolución intermedia (por debajo de 1080 líneas se queda en 3 píxeles). Cada píxel de la pantalla promedia la máscara sobre su propia área, así que una escala no entera no produce muaré. Esto vale para `fakelottes`, `fakelottes-geom`, `crt-pi` y `fake-CRT-Geom` (en el último, su parámetro *Mask Size* se multiplica por el mismo factor); `crt-nes-mini` no tiene máscara y sus scanlines salen de las líneas del propio juego, así que no necesitó cambios. Las scanlines de todos ya siguen las líneas del juego a cualquier resolución. Si añades shaders propios cuya máscara se mida en píxeles de pantalla, escálala por `max(1.0, OutputSize.y / 1080.0)` de la misma forma. Los shaders `.glsl` que se incluyen en `shaders\` **no se han escrito para este programa: proceden de la colección de shaders de RetroArch / libretro** ([glsl-shaders](https://github.com/libretro/glsl-shaders)), y cada uno conserva la autoría y la licencia de su autor. Mira el principio de cada fichero: por ejemplo `crt-pi.glsl` (davej) está bajo la GNU GPL versión 2 o posterior, y varios ficheros solo indican el nombre del autor y no incluyen texto de licencia, así que comprueba su licencia original antes de redistribuirlos. El programa solo los carga en tiempo de ejecución, como ficheros independientes, y nada de él deriva de ellos; los efectos incorporados (Líneas de escaneo, CRT suave, CRT completo) son código propio de este programa. Si redistribuyes el programa con estos shaders, conserva con ellos sus cabeceras y licencias. Sus licencias se aplican solo a esos ficheros, no al resto del programa. Si prefieres no incluirlos, borra los ficheros: el programa funciona sin ellos y los efectos incorporados siguen disponibles. ## Sonido y música - **Sonido del chip**: el YM2149 (3 tonos, ruido, envolvente) se sintetiza a partir de las escrituras de registros del juego con su marca de tiempo dentro del fotograma, así que se mantiene sincronizado con la imagen. El tempo de la música es el que el juego programa en el timer C del MFP (≈48,6 Hz), independiente de la frecuencia de fotogramas. - **Volúmenes**: *Volumen* general más cuatro deslizadores: *Música (Amiga / bancos)* (la del disco Amiga y la de los bancos), *Música (YM2149F)* (las canciones originales del Atari ST), *Efectos muestreados* y *Efectos (YM2149F)* (los efectos que hace el propio chip). Cada uno es una ganancia que se aplica al mezclar el sonido, así que se mueven con suavidad. - **Efectos multicanal** (desactivado por defecto): el original reproduce las muestras de efectos en los canales A y B del chip (una voz cada uno) y una muestra nueva corta la anterior. Con esta opción el programa las mezcla: hasta 8 voces a la frecuencia original (4915,2 Hz) y niveles de 4 bits, leídas con muestreo y retención como el chip. Efectos distintos nunca se cortan entre sí; como máximo suenan 2 instancias de la *misma* muestra a la vez (una tercera apaga la más antigua en 10 ms), lo que evita que los disparos y las explosiones encadenadas se amontonen. Un limitador suave evita la saturación. - **Panorámica estéreo de efectos** (desactivada por defecto): cada efecto se coloca entre los altavoces según la posición horizontal del objeto que lo produce (enemigo, vehículo, explosión, tu arma…) cuando empieza el sonido: borde izquierdo de la zona de juego 100 % izquierda, centro los dos por igual, borde derecho 100 % derecha (lineal). Los orígenes desconocidos se centran. Funciona con o sin *Efectos multicanal*. ### Música: Atari ST, Amiga y bancos de música El elemento **Música** de la pestaña Sonido es una única lista que recorre toda la música disponible: - **Atari ST (original)**: la música del chip del propio juego. El **suavizado subpíxel** dibuja los sprites en su posición intermedia exacta en lugar de redondearla a un píxel entero (no añade fotogramas). Con la interpolación **desactivada**, cada fotograma del juego se muestra tal cual y el retardo es mucho menor, a costa de tirones (60 Hz no es múltiplo de 25, así que los fotogramas alternan entre 2 y 3 refrescos). La **Velocidad del juego** elimina esos tirones: *Original* mantiene 25 fps; *Ajustar al refresco* ejecuta el juego a la frecuencia de fotogramas que divide la frecuencia de refresco (60 Hz: velocidad 1,2×, 30 fotogramas lógicos por segundo, cada uno exactamente 2 refrescos; 144 Hz: 48 VBL/s; 100 Hz: 50, exactamente el original). La música y las muestras mantienen su velocidad normal. **Opciones de latencia** (Latencia): - **Margen de emulación** (`latency`, por defecto 3,6 fotogramas; Re Pág/Av Pág mientras juegas): cuánto se adelanta la emulación a la pantalla. Por debajo de unos 3,6 hay que extrapolar la imagen y el scroll «rebota» al detenerse. - **Lectura rápida de entrada**: el teclado y los mandos se leen unas 1000 veces por segundo en su propio hilo en lugar de una vez por fotograma de pantalla (hasta 16 ms tarde). - **Audio de baja latencia**: búferes pequeños del dispositivo (unos 10 ms a través del mezclador de Windows); el sonido se mantiene sincronizado con la imagen y su retardo total sigue al margen de emulación. El **Ajuste de sincronía del audio** (−100…100 ms) desplaza el sonido más tarde (positivo) o más pronto (negativo) si no cuadra en tu PC. Si no se puede abrir la nueva salida, se mantiene la normal. ## Packs gráficos **El volcado.** `assets/original/` es un volcado completo de los gráficos del juego, tomado directamente de los datos que el juego descomprime en la RAM, como hojas PNG editables en orden canónico, con un `index.json` (número de fotograma, hash del contenido, dirección de memoria y formato de datos de cada celda) y su propio `README.txt`. El programa lo genera solo la primera vez que arranca (juega al juego con entradas guionizadas: intro, título, mapa, tienda y las 12 misiones; unos pocos segundos). Las pantallas son capas que reemplazan solo los píxeles aún iguales a los de la capa original, de modo que los textos, cursores y marcadores los sigue dibujando el juego. Los fundidos de paleta también oscurecen los reemplazos. No se reemplazan: los textos y dígitos, el icono del arma / contadores / vidas de los paneles laterales y los raros sprites cortados por el borde de la pantalla. ## Correcciones del juego Activadas por defecto; `enemy_script_fix: false` ejecuta el juego exactamente como era. No se modifica ningún fichero del juego. - **Script de enemigos** (`$B0B8`): cuando el contador de un enemigo llega a 0 la rutina carga la orden siguiente y **vuelve sin mover al enemigo ese fotograma**, así que cada orden (disparar, girar, cambiar de animación) pierde un fotograma de movimiento. Imperceptible a 25 fps en un Atari; a 60 fps se nota como microtirones (también ocurre en Hatari). El parche convierte el `RTS` de `$B13E` en un `BRA.B` a `$B0C6`. La duración de las órdenes no cambia; los enemigos recorren ~1 px más por orden. - **Controlador de sonido**: mientras suena un efecto muestreado, el controlador deja de escribir los registros de los canales A y B de la música y el registro de ruido. Se parchean tres saltos condicionales (`$41EE2`, `$41EF8`, `$41F32`) para que la música siga sonando, y las escrituras de registros del propio efecto van a un canal de síntesis aparte. - **Explosiones en niveles de scroll horizontal**: el paso del scroll horizontal (`$49A0`) olvida la lista de explosiones (`$1472`), así que las explosiones y la gran bola de fuego se quedaban fijas en pantalla mientras el escenario se desplazaba. Un gancho justo antes del `RTS` de esa rutina añade el paso que falta. - `scroll_fix` estabiliza la presentación del scroll horizontal (véase [Referencia de configuración](#referencia-de-configuración)). ## Guardado El juego original no tiene función de guardado, así que el port almacena instantáneas completas de la máquina en `saves/`. Usa **Juego → Ranura de guardado / Guardar partida / Cargar partida** (3 ranuras, con fecha) desde el mapa, la tienda o en mitad de una misión. si no, `music_pack` es el banco, `@amiga` para el disco Amiga) | | `fast_input`, `low_latency_audio`, `audio_sync_trim_ms` | sección Latencia | | `graphics_pack` | pack gráfico elegido | | `pad_dual_stick` | modo doble stick: el derecho apunta (por defecto `true`) | | `pad_aim_autofire` | el stick derecho también mantiene el disparo mientras está pulsado (por defecto `true`) | | `key_up`, `key_fire`, … | teclas como códigos de tecla virtual de Windows (Ctrl = 17) | | `pad_fire`, … | botones del mando por nombre: `"A"`, `"RT"`, `"Start"`…, `"none"` | ## Solución de problemas - **«No se encuentran los datos del juego»** (la pantalla que muestra el juego cuando no tiene con qué arrancar): para Windows o una compilación Linux independiente, coloca `DOW` (CRC32 de referencia `6703B50F`) o una imagen `.st` con CRC32 `F6E84D7A` directamente en `original\` / `original/`. La AppImage de Linux lee cualquiera de los ficheros desde `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dogs-of-war/original/` (normalmente `~/.local/share/dogs-of-war/original/`) o usa por defecto su `original/DOW` incluido. - **No hay sonido en Linux**: deja `SDL_AUDIODRIVER` sin definir para que SDL seleccione un backend disponible (normalmente el servicio compatible con PulseAudio del escritorio, incluido PipeWire, o ALSA). `error.log` muestra el driver seleccionado. - **El sonido crepita o se retrasa**: sube el margen de emulación (Re Pág) o desactiva *Audio de baja latencia*; `error.log` lista los cortes de audio. - **Tirones a 60 Hz**: deja activada la *Interpolación de fotogramas*, o usa *Velocidad del juego → Ajustar al refresco* con la interpolación desactivada. - **Un pack gráfico no hace nada**: solo reemplaza las celdas que difieren de `assets/original/`; borra esa carpeta para regenerar el volcado y comprueba los nombres y tamaños de las hojas. - **Si el estado del juego se corrompe** (salta a código basura) el port vuelve automáticamente a una instantánea de unos segundos antes y escribe `saves/crashN_inicio.dows`, `crashN_entradas.txt` y `crashN_fin.dows` (la instantánea, tus entradas desde entonces y el estado corrupto) además de un informe en `error.log`. ## Cómo funciona - **El juego**: su programa 68000 está traducido a C (`source/generated/`, una función C por rutina, ejecutándose como fibras cooperativas). Si alguna vez el juego salta a una dirección que no es código del juego (un estado corrupto) el port vuelve a una instantánea de unos segundos antes y lo registra (véase Solución de problemas). - **La máquina** (`tos.c`, `runtime/machine.c`): un Atari STE con un mini-TOS (justo el GEMDOS/BIOS/XBIOS que necesita el juego), teclado y joystick IKBD/ACIA, timers del MFP y zonas de paleta por línea de escaneo. En cada arranque `boot.c` construye la memoria que deja el cargador original (`RUNME.TOS` y `HAGA`) cuando salta al juego. Todo el código 68000, el del cargador incluido, ya es C, así que la fuente original solo aporta los datos del juego; las pocas variables del cargador que lee el código están en el programa. - **Captura de escena** (`scene.c`): para cada fotograma lógico registra el fondo (búfer circular de scroll), el HUD y cada objeto dibujado (enemigos, jugador, balas, explosiones, vehículos…) con su posición, y mantiene un **atlas de sprites**. - **Presentador** (`render.c`, `present.c`): dibuja cualquier instante entre dos fotogramas lógicos, con scroll y sprites en posiciones intermedias, filtros del movimiento de los enemigos y estabilización del scroll. - **Salida**: `video.c` (Win32 + OpenGL 3.3), `ym.c`, `mixer.c`, `mp3.c` (minimp3 / stb_vorbis / lector WAV incluidos), `audioout.c` (waveOut / WASAPI), `menu.c` (`port/ui2d.c` portable), `input.c` (XInput), `cfg.c`, `gfxpack.c`, `dump.c`. - **Verificación**: la traducción se comprobó contra un emulador 68000 independiente, instrucción por instrucción y fotograma a fotograma, en las 12 misiones (los 4 MB de RAM completos, los registros de sonido y la paleta). ## Compilación desde el código fuente Todo está en `source/` (véase `source/README.md`). En Windows, instala Zig, MinGW-w64 o Clang y ejecuta `source\build.bat`; escribe `build\dowport.exe`. En Debian/Ubuntu Linux, instala `build-essential pkg-config libsdl2-dev` y ejecuta `bash source/build-linux.sh`; escribe `build/dowport`. ## Estado Funciona: arranque desde los ficheros originales, título, menús, mapa de misiones, tienda y las 12 misiones con interpolación a 60 fps en Windows y Linux. Las compilaciones x64 de ambas plataformas están disponibles en la [última versión](https://github.com/voodatari/Dogs-of-War-Atari-ST-Recomp/releases/latest). Créditos: Claude Sonnet 5.5 y VooD.

# Screamer Reverse Engineering

This project reconstructs the DOS game Screamer (1995) into rebuildable
source code.  The reference artifact is the GOG.com distribution for macOS.
The first target is the original DOS platform.  Later targets are modern
platforms, starting with the current host (macOS on arm64).

## Status

Initial reconnaissance is complete.  The project has:

- a documented inventory of the distribution and the installed game,
- a parser and disassembler for the DOS/4GW linear executables (`tools/le.py`),
- a CD image extractor (`tools/extract_cd_image.py`),
- an inventory generator (`tools/inventory.py`),
- a rebuild store with one record per function and its status
  (`tools/rebuild/store.py`),
- a check runner that builds and tests the declared checks
  (`tools/rebuild/run.py`),
- a strict identity gate and a whole-image oracle
  (`--strict`, `tools/rebuild/oracle.py`, and
  `tools/rebuild/image_compare.py`),
- a self-contained status page of the store (`tools/rebuild/view.py`), published
  to GitHub Pages at <https://i-zhirov.github.io/screamer_re/>,
- a generated program map with a drift check (`tools/rebuild/docs.py`),
- a named call graph with a drift check (`tools/rebuild/callgraph.py`),
- decoders for the graphics assets and the sound formats,
- an investigation log with evidence and open questions.

Reconstructed module sources exist under `tools/rebuild/`.  One function,
`memcpy`, matches the original byte for byte.  The other modules hold a recorded
difference or a shape match.

## Repository layout

```text
AGENTS.md   conventions for AI agents
docs/       project documentation
  explanation/  findings and roadmap
  reference/    distribution, inventory, formats, executables, tooling
tools/      analysis tools
work/       extracted artifacts and generated output (not in git)
task.md     the original task definition
```

## Quick start

The game runs on the host through the installed GOG bundle:

```sh
open ~/Documents/Screamer.app
```

The bundle carries a universal DOSBox binary.  On Apple silicon it runs
through Rosetta 2.

Inspect a DOS/4GW linear executable:

```sh
python3 tools/le.py info ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE
python3 tools/le.py map  ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE 0x300f8
python3 tools/le.py disasm ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE 0x300f8
python3 tools/le.py calls ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE 0x300f8
python3 tools/le.py tree  ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE 0x300f8
python3 tools/le.py targets ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE 0x10020 0x300be
```

Run the strict byte gate and the whole-image oracle:

```sh
python3 tools/rebuild/run.py run --all --strict
python3 tools/rebuild/run.py run --recheck-record 0x300ec
python3 tools/rebuild/image_compare.py \
  --original ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE \
  --rebuilt work/rebuild/STARTH.EXE
```

Find the program entry at run time.  The tool needs DOSBox-X:

```sh
python3 tools/entry_probe.py \
  --game-dir ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game
```

Extract the data track of the CD image:

```sh
python3 tools/extract_cd_image.py \
  ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/SCREAM.DAT \
  work/screamer_data_track.iso
```

Build a file inventory with SHA-256 digests:

```sh
python3 tools/inventory.py \
  ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game
```

Run the full pipeline end to end.  The check needs Docker, DOSBox-X, a built
driver artifact, and the installed Ghidra loader, and takes about 8 minutes
plus the Ghidra import:

```sh
python3 tools/rebuild/harness.py build --module driver
nix develop .#cross-check --command python3 tools/pipeline_check.py \
  --game-dir ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game
```

Run the three-tool cross-check alone.  It prints four fact lines and writes the
raw tool output under `work/cross-check/`:

```sh
nix develop .#cross-check --command python3 tools/cross_check.py \
  --original ~/Documents/Screamer.app/Contents/Resources/game/STARTH.EXE \
  --main 0x10020 --call-site 0xd4364 --work-root work
```

## Development environment

The project tools run inside a Nix shell:

```sh
nix develop
r2 -v
```

`flake.nix` and `flake.lock` pin Python, capstone, and radare2.  DOSBox-X comes
from Homebrew.  The `ghidra` shell carries Ghidra with the LX/LE loader:

```sh
nix develop .#ghidra --command sh tools/ghidra/install_loader.sh
nix develop .#ghidra --command sh tools/ghidra/decompile.sh 0x10020 0x2ecf8
```

The `cross-check` shell carries Python, capstone, radare2, Ghidra, `curl`,
and `unzip`.  The full check runs there.  Install the loader once per user:

```sh
nix develop .#cross-check --command sh tools/ghidra/install_loader.sh
```

## Checks

The full check runs every stage in the `cross-check` shell and reports
399 checks.  `--skip-cross` skips stage 8 and the tool preflight, so the run
reports 395 checks.  `--skip-runtime` skips stages 5, 6, 7, and 9 and still
runs stage 8, so the run reports 384 checks.  Both flags report 380 checks.
The record run skips a record whose input fingerprint still matches its
recorded result, so after one full run the record run takes only the hashing
time for the unchanged modules.  `--strict` turns the identity check into a
byte gate: the relocation-aware oracle masks the fixup slots and the direct
branch targets, so `free` and `exit` pass, and a reordered or shape-only match
fails.  `--recheck-record ADDR`
forces one fresh run and prints the full check output.  `store.py check`
validates every record and module against the JSON Schema contracts.  Stage 11
also runs the whole-image oracle when `--rebuilt-image` exists, and reports a
skip when no whole image is built.  CI runs the syntax gate and the unit suite
on every push and pull request, and the full check on a self-hosted runner.
The pre-commit hook regenerates the status page; enable the hooks once per clone:

```sh
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
```

On a push to `master`, the `status` job packages the page for GitHub Pages, and
the `deploy` job runs after the syntax gate.  Pull requests upload the
`rebuild-status` artifact but do not deploy.  The published page is
<https://i-zhirov.github.io/screamer_re/>.  The Pages source is
`GitHub Actions` in the repository settings.

The full check needs the game directory, DOSBox-X, and the installed Ghidra
loader.  Set `SCREAMER_GAME_DIR` to use another game directory.

GitHub Actions runs the syntax gate on every push and pull request.  The full
check runs on a self-hosted runner that holds the game, DOSBox-X, Nix, and the
loader.  Register the runner with the labels `macOS` and `screamer-artifacts`,
and set the repository variable `SCREAMER_SELF_HOSTED` to `true` to enable that
job.

## Documentation

- [Findings](docs/explanation/findings.md) — evidence-backed observations
  and open questions.
- [Roadmap](docs/explanation/roadmap.md) — milestones and the
  reconstruction plan.
- [Distribution](docs/reference/distribution.md) — GOG package and
  installed bundle layout.
- [Inventory](docs/reference/inventory.md) — game files with sizes and
  SHA-256 digests.
- [Executables](docs/reference/executables.md) — linear executable
  metadata.
- [Program map](docs/reference/program-map.md) — the recovered startup
  path and the program functions.
- [File formats](docs/reference/file-formats.md) — observed data formats.
- [Tooling](docs/reference/tooling.md) — tools, commands, and limits.

# RedCat's Razende Rekenrace: reverse engineering and port A study of the 1996 DOS game **RedCat's Razende Rekenrace** (Davilex), a racing game for primary-school arithmetic, and a reimplementation in C that plays it on Linux and in the browser. ![The port: the start lights go out, Brutus and Snitch pull away, and RedCat drives down the canyon past the cacti and a ramp](docs/media/redcat-race.gif) The research half is notes on how the original works, worked out from its executables (Watcom C, DOS/4GW) and its data, and from experiments with it running under DOSBox-X. Each finding records the code addresses it rests on and how sure it is. The port is a new engine in C (SDL2) that reads the original game data unchanged. It plays the game's round as the original does: the intro film, the menu, the races, the four kinds of arithmetic exercises in between, the podium and the high scores. The same sources build for the web with Emscripten.

All of these are the port, captured in the first world, De Welkomstrace. **The game itself is not included.** You need your own copy of the CD. Nothing here changes or redistributes the original files. ## Playing You need CMake, a C compiler and SDL2. Point the launcher at the game's data: the CD root, or the installed `C:\DAVILEX\RCREKEN` (the directory with `RCS.IND`, `RC.IND` and `TRANS.DAT`): ```sh port/play.sh # the whole game, intro first port/play.sh --no-intro # straight to the menu port/play.sh --race # straight into a race ``` It builds the port the first time. The game directory is only read: the record (`RRRIO.INF`), the pupils' results and the high scores go to `~/.local/share/Davilex/RedCat`, or to the directory given with `--save`. The other options are in [`port/README.md`](port/README.md). ### In the browser ```sh port/web/build.sh # needs Emscripten (emcc) port/web/serve.sh # then open http://localhost:8080/redcat.html ``` The page asks for your game folder (the CD or the installed game) once and keeps the files it needs in the browser's storage. ## Layout | Path | Contents | |---|---| | `research/discoveries.md` | What has been established, with evidence | | `research/hypotheses.md` | Ideas that are not settled yet | | `research/open-questions.md` | Open and resolved questions | | `reverse-engineering/` | Reference docs: executables, file formats, architecture, running the original under DOSBox-X | | `reverse-engineering/tools/` | LE loader, disassembler, function finder, xrefs, Unicorn emulation and the DOSBox-X driver | | `reverse-engineering/analysis/` | Function lists, names, CD inventory | | `port/` | The C port; [`port/README.md`](port/README.md) is its detailed manual | | `port/web/` | The WebAssembly build | | `port/rctools/` | Python tools for the game's archives, images and maps | ## How the research works Each finding carries a label: CONFIRMED, STRONGLY SUPPORTED, LIKELY or SPECULATIVE. The notes never present an inference as fact. Evidence from the binaries and from runtime experiments comes before outside documentation. Where the port's behaviour comes from the original, its source comments name the address it was taken from, for example `0x1103e` for the start lights. Where the port deliberately differs, `port/README.md` says so. The working rules, and how to set up `.work/`, are in [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md). The 32-bit programs are LE executables, which most tools do not open. `reverse-engineering/tools/leparse.py` applies their fixups and writes each as an ELF image at its run-time addresses. The original runs in a patched DOSBox-X that `reverse-engineering/tools/dosrun.py` drives on a hidden display: keys, screenshots, memory and save states; see [`reverse-engineering/runtime-dosbox.md`](reverse-engineering/runtime-dosbox.md). The tools need Python 3 with `capstone`, and some `unicorn`. ## Status The game's round is playable from the intro to the high scores. Not ported yet: the winner's film after a world's last race (the podium stands in), the closing film, the menu's joystick set-up and the mouse pointer in the exercises. The unanswered questions are in `research/open-questions.md`. ## License This software is released under the [BOLA License](LICENSE). It covers this project's own code and notes, not the game. ## Legal RedCat's Razende Rekenrace, its data and its box art (Davilex Software BV, 1996; the cover image is from MobyGames) are the property of their rights holders. This project contains no game data and is meant for people who own the game.
